cards.front: Recall a key point about The Role of the Media
cards.back: A free press is essential for democracy: it holds power to account (investigative journalism exposed the MPs' expenses scandal), informs citizens (enabling informed voting), and provides a platform for debate. Freedom of the press is protected under Article 10 of the ECHR (freedom of expression).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Role of the Media
cards.back: Media regulation: Ofcom regulates broadcasting (TV, radio) - can impose fines and revoke licences. IPSO (Independent Press Standards Organisation) regulates newspapers - handles complaints but cannot impose fines. Some argue regulation should be stronger (Leveson Inquiry after phone-hacking scandal recommended statutory regulation of the press, but this was not fully implemented).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Role of the Media
cards.back: Media bias: all media has some bias - editorial choices about what to cover and how to frame stories. Newspaper bias: most UK national newspapers support conservative or right-wing positions (The Sun, Daily Mail, Telegraph). Broadcasters (BBC, ITV, Channel 4) are required by Ofcom to be impartial. Social media: algorithms create filter bubbles (users see content that reinforces their views).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Role of the Media
cards.back: Fake news and misinformation: deliberately false information presented as news. Spread rapidly on social media. Impact: undermines trust in institutions, distorts public debate, and can influence elections. The UK government has established the Counter Disinformation Unit; Ofcom has new duties under the Online Safety Act 2023 to protect users from harmful content.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Role of the Media
cards.back: Social media and citizenship: enables citizen journalism, activism (#MeToo, Black Lives Matter), and political engagement. However: enables misinformation, online abuse, and echo chambers. The Online Safety Act 2023 requires platforms to protect users from illegal content and content harmful to children.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — the role of the media?
cards.back: 1. For The Role of the Media questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link The Role of the Media to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether the UK media supports or undermines democracy.

AO1 (Knowledge & Understanding — 30%): You need to demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the role of the media, including key concepts, legal frameworks, and institutional structures. AO2 (Analysis & Evaluation — 40%): You must analyse and evaluate different viewpoints, policies, and approaches related to the role of the media. cards.front: Understanding The Role of the Media in British Context
cards.back: The Role of the Media is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues.

cards.front: The Role of the Media and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding the role of the media requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and The Role of the Media
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
